title: Arrays, vectors and dynamic allocation
description: Static arrays and pointer arithmetic, arrays of pointers and pointers to arrays, new[] and delete[], and std::vector.

content.title: Static arrays and pointer arithmetic
content.body:
int a[5]; is an array of 5 ints whose size must be known at compile time. A local array is not initialized; int a[5] = {1, 2}; sets the rest to 0.

- In most expressions, the name of an array decays into a pointer to its first element. sizeof(a) and &a are the exceptions.
- a[i] is exactly *(a + i): adding 1 to a pointer moves it by one element, not one byte.
- A function parameter written int a[10] is really int* a: the size is lost.
- Arrays cannot be assigned, incremented or returned by value.
- There is no bounds checking: reading or writing outside the array is undefined behaviour. A pointer one past the last element is allowed, but must not be dereferenced.
- int a[n] with a variable n is not standard C++ (g++ accepts it as an extension).

content.explanation: In main, sizeof(arr) is the size of the whole array: 40 / 4 = 10. The parameter int a[10] is really int* a, so in print, sizeof(a) is the size of a pointer: 8 / 4 = 2. This is why functions that take a C array also need its size, or should take a std::vector or std::array instead.
p starts at a[1]. *p++ prints 20, then moves p to a[2]. *++p first moves p to a[3], then prints 40. p[1] is *(p + 1), a[4] = 50, and *(p - 2) is a[1] = 20.

choices.text: It does not compile: 2[a] is not valid

content.explanation: a[i] is defined as *(a + i), and addition is commutative, so 2[a] is *(2 + a), which is a[2] = 3. Never write this in real code. * binds tighter than -, and - tighter than <<, so the second value is a[3] - a[0] = 4 - 1 = 3.

choices.text: b = a;
int d[n];

content.explanation: Arrays cannot be assigned (b = a) or incremented (a++): an array is not a pointer, even though its name decays into one. int d[n] is a variable-length array, which is not standard C++ because n is not a compile-time constant (g++ only accepts it as an extension and warns with -pedantic). int c[] deduces a size of 2, and b + 3 is a valid one-past-the-end pointer.

content.title: Arrays of pointers and pointers to arrays
content.body:
To read a declaration, start from the name, go right, then left, and read what is in parentheses first.

- int* a[3]: a is an array of 3 pointers to int.
- int (*p)[3]: p is a pointer to an array of 3 ints.
- &arr has the type int (*)[N]: adding 1 to it skips the whole array, while arr + 1 skips one element.
- int m[2][3] is 2 rows of 3 ints stored one after the other. m decays into int (*)[3], a pointer to its first row, not into int**.
- A function taking a 2D array is written void f(int m[][3]) or void f(int (*m)[3]). Only the first size can be left out.
- const char* names[] = {"Ann", "Bob"}; is an array of pointers to string literals.

content.question:
int (*p)[4];

What is p?

choices.text: An array of 4 pointers to int
A pointer to an array of 4 ints
A pointer to a function that returns an int
A pointer to an int, initialized to 4

content.explanation: The parentheses bind * to p first: p is a pointer, and what it points to is an int[4]. Without the parentheses, int* p[4] would be an array of 4 pointers to int.

Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the pointed type. a decays into an int*, so a + 1 is 4 bytes further. q points to an int[4], so q + 1 is sizeof(int[4]) = 16 bytes further. The casts to char* measure the difference in bytes.
[] binds tighter than *, so *ptrs[1] is *(ptrs[1]), which is y. ptrs[2] = ptrs[0] makes the third pointer point to x, without changing z. *ptrs[2] += 5 therefore adds 5 to x.

choices.text: It does not compile: m cannot be stored in an int (*)[3]

content.explanation: m decays into a pointer to its first row, an int (*)[3], so row[1][0] is m[1][0] = 4. *(*(m + 1) + 2) is m[1][2] = 6. **m is m[0][0] = 1, and the + 1 applies to that value, giving 2 (it is not m[1][0]).

choices.text: int** p2 = m;
f(a);
g(m);
f(m);
h(m);

content.explanation: m decays into int (*)[3], a pointer to rows of 3 ints, not into int**: a 2D array contains no pointers at all. g and h take the same type, int (*)[3]. a is an array of pointers, so it decays into int**, which f accepts.

choices.text: 3 Cleo ob
3 C ob
3 C Bob
11 C ob

content.explanation: names is an array of 3 pointers, whatever the length of the strings. *names[2] is *(names[2]): the first char of "Cleo". names[1] + 1 is a const char* to the second char of "Bob", and << prints a const char* as a string from there: ob.

content.title: Dynamic allocation with new and delete
content.body:
new allocates on the heap and returns a pointer. The memory stays until it is freed explicitly.

- new int(5) is freed with delete. new int[n] is freed with delete[]. Mixing them up is undefined behaviour.
- With new[], n can be computed at run time. new int[n] leaves the values uninitialized; new int[n]() sets them to 0.
- delete must receive exactly the pointer that new returned. Deleting nullptr does nothing; deleting twice is undefined behaviour.
- delete does not set the pointer to nullptr: the pointer dangles.
- When new cannot allocate, it throws std::bad_alloc. It does not return nullptr, unless you use new (std::nothrow).
- A dynamic 2D array can be an array of pointers: new int*[rows], then new int[cols] for each row. Free each row, then the array of rows.
- A class that owns a raw pointer must define its copy operations (rule of three), or use std::vector or smart pointers instead.

content.question: Which snippets have undefined behaviour?

choices.text:
int* p = new int[5];
delete p;

int* p = nullptr;
delete p;

content.explanation: delete on memory from new[] is a mismatch. delete[] must receive the exact pointer returned by new[], not one that was moved. p[3] reads past the end of a 3-element array. Deleting nullptr is allowed. Deleting through a copy of the pointer is fine as long as it happens only once. new int[3]() initializes the values to 0, so p[2] is 0.

choices.text: Nothing special: b gets its own copy of the 10 ints
It does not compile: Buffer has no copy constructor
Undefined behaviour: both objects delete[] the same memory at the end of main
A memory leak, but no undefined behaviour

content.explanation: The copy constructor generated by the compiler copies the pointer, not the array it points to (a shallow copy). At the end of main, b and then a both run delete[] on the same memory. You should either define the copy constructor and copy assignment (rule of three), or replace int* by std::vector<int>, which copies correctly.

choices.text: delete[] grid;

content.explanation: Every new[] needs its own delete[], in reverse order. Deleting only grid leaks every row. Deleting grid first and then reading grid[i] uses freed memory. delete instead of delete[] on memory from new[] is undefined behaviour. A std::vector<std::vector<int>> avoids all of this.

choices.text: p is nullptr and the message is printed
new throws std::bad_alloc, so the if is never reached
p points to a smaller block
It is undefined behaviour

content.explanation: A plain new never returns nullptr: it throws std::bad_alloc, which you can catch. Only int* p = new (std::nothrow) int[hugeNumber]; returns nullptr when it fails, and then this check makes sense.

content.title: std::vector
content.body:
std::vector<T> is a dynamic array that manages its own memory: its elements are contiguous, and they are freed automatically (RAII).

- size() is the number of elements, capacity() the room already allocated. reserve(n) increases the capacity without changing the size.
- When push_back needs more capacity, the vector allocates a bigger block and moves its elements there. Every pointer, reference and iterator to its elements is then invalid.
- v[i] does not check bounds (undefined behaviour when out of range); v.at(i) throws std::out_of_range.
- std::vector<int> v(3, 7) holds three 7s, while v{3, 7} holds 3 and 7: braces prefer the initializer list.
- Passed by value, a vector is copied. Pass it by const reference to read it, or by reference to modify it.
- v.data() gives a pointer to the first element, for functions that expect a C array.
- For a fixed size known at compile time, std::array<int, 5> is a safer replacement for int[5].

content.explanation: Parentheses call the size constructors: a holds three 7s, c holds three 0s. Braces prefer the initializer_list constructor: b holds the two values 3 and 7, d holds the single value 3.

choices.text: It prints 11
It does not compile: you cannot keep a reference to a vector element
Undefined behaviour if push_back reallocates (very likely here): first and p would point to freed memory
It prints 11, because the vector updates references when it reallocates

content.explanation: A vector created from 3 values usually has a capacity of 3, so push_back must allocate a new block, move the elements and free the old one. first and p still point to the old block. Calling reserve beforehand, or keeping indexes instead of pointers, avoids the problem.

choices.text: The try block prints B
v[3] = 1 is undefined behaviour: operator[] does not check bounds
v[3] = 1 grows the vector to 4 elements
The try block prints AB

content.explanation: v has 3 elements, indexes 0 to 2. at(3) throws std::out_of_range before anything is assigned, so A is never printed. operator[] never checks bounds and never grows the vector: writing v[3] is undefined behaviour. Use push_back or resize to add elements.

choices.text: show does not compile: v is a reference to a const vector
Without show, the program prints 1
Without show, the program prints 2
fillRef does not compile: a function cannot modify its caller's vector

content.explanation: push_back is not a const member function, so it cannot be called through a const reference. fill receives a copy, so its push_back does not affect main's v. fillRef receives a reference, so it adds the only element that v ends up with.

In a const vector, the elements are const: v[0] is an int* const, a pointer that cannot change but still points to a modifiable int, so *v[0] = 5 compiles. In w, the vector is not const, so its pointers can change, but each one points to a const int, so *w[0] cannot be modified.
